title: Climate shock becomes economic adaptation
subtitle: Gulf of Maine, 1815–1820
description: A volcanic-climate shock altered temperatures, fish phenology and food pressure; fishers shifted effort and the emergency response became a lasting economic transition.

title: Weather shock becomes a subsistence crisis
subtitle: Czech Lands, 1816–1817
description: Cold and persistent wet weather damaged grain production; the harvest shock propagated into food scarcity and grain-price pressure with a measurable lag into 1817.

title: Cold years store risk in the water system
subtitle: Alpine Rhine Basin, 1816–1817
description: Post-eruption cold and snow conditions increased snow storage. In 1817, spring snowfall, snowmelt and intense rain combined in major Rhine and Lake Constance flooding.

title: Climate becomes cultural context
subtitle: Geneva, summer 1816
description: The unusually cold and cloudy Geneva summer created the documented setting in which Mary Godwin's literary circle stayed indoors, exchanged ghost stories and generated the story that became Frankenstein.

title: The same volcanic forcing, a different regional expression
subtitle: Qing China, 1816
description: Proxy evidence shows severe cold, frost, snow and ice in southern China while hydroclimate evidence is spatially mixed, illustrating why WorldThreads must preserve regional variation and proxy disagreement.

title: Direct eruption damage disrupts local livelihoods
subtitle: Sumbawa and neighboring islands, 1815 antecedent
description: Local food, water and maritime disruption form a branching thread. Recovery through 1816 remains a research gap.
